submission.title: The Perfect Lie
submission.full_story:
The business card shouldn't have existed—David worked in tech, not finance, and his name definitely wasn't Marcus Webb.

Sarah stared at her husband's photograph smiling back at her from the glossy cardstock. She'd only been looking for tissues in his jacket pocket.

Her fingers shook as she dialed.

"Webb Financial Services."

"Marcus Webb, please."

"We don't have a Marcus Webb."

Sarah's pulse hammered. "Dark hair, brown eyes, six-foot-two?"

"Oh, the temp from last month! But his name was Jake. Kept to himself, paid in cash."

The phone clattered to the floor.

Jake. Not David. Not her husband of two years.

Her wedding photos lined the mantle—his arm around her waist, his lips on her forehead, his promises whispered in her ear. All lies?

The apartment key scraped in the lock.

"Sarah?" His voice, warm and familiar, the same voice that said "I love you" every morning. "I brought takeout from that place you like."

She pressed the business card against her chest, feeling her heartbeat through the paper.

The man walking through their door knew her coffee order, her childhood fears, her body. He had access to everything—their bank account, her passwords, her trust.

But she didn't even know his real name.

The footsteps stopped. "Babe? You okay?"
submission.short_summary: Sarah finds a business card in her husband David's jacket with his photo but a different name—Marcus Webb. When she calls the number, she discovers that no Marcus Webb works there, but they remember a temp named Jake who matches David's description. As her husband comes home, Sarah realizes she may not know his real name, leaving her questioning everything about their marriage.

submission.title: The Perfect Lie
submission.full_story:
"Jake."

The word stopped him cold. David's keys clattered to the floor, takeout bags forgotten in his hands.

Sarah held up the business card, her wedding ring catching the light. "That's who you really are, isn't it?"

The color drained from his face. For two years, she'd memorized every expression—his morning smile, his concentrated frown, his guilty look when he ate her leftovers. This was different. This was fear.

"Sarah, please—"

"I called them." Her voice was steady, but her hands shook. "Webb Financial. They said you worked there one month. Paid in cash. No records, no references."

He set down the bags with careful precision. "Let me explain."

"Explain what? That I've been sleeping next to a stranger? That our entire marriage is built on lies?"

"Not lies. I never lied about loving you."

"But everything else?"

He ran his hands through his hair—a gesture she'd found endearing yesterday, terrifying today. "My real name is Jake Morrison. I was an accountant in Chicago."

"Was?"

"I discovered my firm was laundering money for some very dangerous people. When I tried to report it..." He touched a scar above his left eyebrow she'd never noticed. "They made it clear I should disappear."

Sarah's grip tightened on the card. "So you became David Chen."

"I became the man who could love you without putting you in danger."

"Danger?" The word hit her like ice water. "What kind of danger?"

His eyes met hers, and she saw the truth before he spoke it.

"The kind that follows you home."
submission.short_summary: Sarah confronts David with the business card, demanding the truth about his real identity. The confrontation reveals his name is actually Jake Morrison, and he's been hiding from dangerous people who want him dead after he discovered their money laundering operation. Just as Sarah thinks she understands the scope of his deception, Jake reveals the terrifying truth: the danger has followed him to their doorstep.

submission.title: The Perfect Lie
submission.full_story:
The black sedan had been watching their building for three hours.

Sarah pressed against the kitchen window, studying the two men in dark suits. Behind her, Jake paced like a caged animal, phone pressed to his ear.

"We leave tonight," he said, hanging up. "I have a contact in Seattle—"

"No." The word came out stronger than she felt. "I'm done being a passenger in my own life."

Jake froze. "Sarah, you don't understand. These people—"

"Kill witnesses. I got that part." She turned from the window, facing the stranger with her husband's face. "What I don't understand is why you thought dragging me into this was love."

His hands shook as he reached for her. "Because losing you would have killed me."

"So instead you're going to get me killed?"

The building's front door buzzed. Once. Twice. Three times.

Jake's face drained of color. "The fire escape—"

"I said no." Sarah walked to their wedding photo on the mantle, studying the smiling couple who'd believed in forever. "I spent two years being the woman you needed me to be. Trusting. Naive. Safe."

The buzzing stopped. Footsteps echoed in the stairwell.

"Sarah, please—"

She picked up the business card that had started it all. Then she looked at Jake—really looked at him. Past the fear, past the lies, to the man who still made her coffee every morning.

"I'm not her anymore," she whispered.

The footsteps stopped outside their door.

Sarah walked to the front door, Jake's panicked breathing behind her. Her hand hovered over the deadbolt.

"Trust me," she said, and opened the door.

Two men. Cold eyes. The taller one's smile never reached his face.

"Mrs. Chen. We need to speak with your husband about some financial discrepancies."

Sarah met his gaze without flinching. "My husband died in a car accident last month."

She closed the door. Turned the deadbolt. Leaned against the wood until her legs stopped shaking.

Jake stared at her like she'd just raised the dead.

"Now," she said, "you're going to tell me everything. And then we're going to disappear together."

submission.title: The Perfect Lie: Before David
submission.full_story:
Jake Morrison found the blood under his fingernails at 2:47 AM.

He'd been clawing at his desk for hours, staring at numbers that shouldn't exist. Fifteen million dollars flowing through Meridian Financial like water through a sieve. Clean money in, dirty money out, and Jake's signature on every transaction.

His coffee mug sat forgotten, contents long cold, as he traced the pattern. Shell companies. Ninety-day lifespans. All roads leading to Kozlov Holdings.

Everyone in Chicago knew that name, even if they pretended not to.

"Working late, Morrison?"

The voice made Jake's soul leave his body. Marcus Webb stood in the doorway—his mentor, his friend, the man who'd saved him from student debt and dead-end interviews.

"Reviewing the Meridian account." Jake's hand moved toward the mouse, ready to close the screen.

Marcus stepped closer, designer shoes silent on carpet. "Find anything... interesting?"

The office felt like a coffin. Jake noticed details that had been invisible for three years: Marcus's watch cost more than Jake's car. His suit was Italian. His smile had never once reached his eyes.

"Everything looks clean," Jake whispered.

"Good." Marcus placed a paternal hand on Jake's shoulder. "You know, curiosity killed the cat. And in our business, some questions are better left unasked."

His grip tightened. "Especially when you have so much to lose. Emma's working late at the gallery tonight, isn't she? Pretty girl. Walks home alone through Grant Park."

Jake's blood turned to ice water.

"Lock up when you're finished. And Jake?" Marcus's smile was razor-thin. "Delete those backup files. All of them."

The door clicked shut like a coffin lid.

Jake stared at his reflection in the black computer screen. He could delete everything. Keep his job, his life, his ignorance. Stay Jake Morrison forever.

Or he could copy the files to a flash drive and kill Jake Morrison tonight.

His finger trembled over the mouse.

The choice would haunt him for the rest of his life—however long that might be.
submission.short_summary: Jake Morrison discovers his accounting firm is laundering money for dangerous criminals. When his mentor threatens his girlfriend Emma, Jake must choose between deleting the evidence and staying safe, or copying the files and destroying his identity forever.

submission.title: The Perfect Lie: Sarah's Choice
submission.full_story:
Sarah Martinez was twenty-four when she learned that love could be a lie.

"I have to tell you something." Michael's voice cracked across their anniversary dinner. Two years together. A ring hidden in his jacket pocket that she'd glimpsed that morning.

Her heart hammered with anticipation. "What is it?"

"I've been seeing someone else. For eight months."

The restaurant noise faded to white static. She watched his mouth move—excuses, apologies, explanations that sounded like Charlie Brown's teacher. Her engagement ring fantasy crumbled into ash.

"Sarah? Did you hear me?"

She heard everything. How he'd fallen out of love. How the other woman understood him better. How he'd wanted to tell her sooner but didn't want to hurt her.

"I thought..." Her voice came out small, broken. "I thought we were getting engaged."

His face crumpled. "I'm sorry. I never meant for this to happen."

But he had meant it. Every secret text, every late work night, every lie told with a straight face while she planned their future.

Walking home alone, Sarah made a promise to herself: never again would she be the fool who didn't see it coming.

For years, she built walls. First dates became interrogations. She investigated boyfriends like a detective, searching for signs of deception. She demanded transparency, access to phones, explanations for every inconsistency.

Men called her paranoid. Controlling. Crazy.

They weren't wrong.

Then David Chen walked into her coffee shop with kind eyes and patient answers. He gave her his phone without being asked. Shared his location. Never made her feel foolish for needing proof.

"I understand," he said when she explained her trust issues. "I want you to feel safe with me."

For two years, he made her feel safe. Cherished. Like the naive girl she'd been before Michael destroyed her faith in love.

She never suspected that David's transparency was the most elaborate lie of all.

The irony would have been funny if it hadn't nearly killed her.

Sometimes the person you trust most is the one with the most to hide.
submission.short_summary: A prequel exploring Sarah's past, revealing the moment that shaped her into the trusting woman Jake would later fall in love with - and the trauma that made her desperate to believe in perfect love.
